g1.correct: traces left by things like posts, likes and searches
accept: traces left by things like posts, likes and searches
g1.label: 1. What does the text say a “digital footprint” is built from?
g1.why: The first paragraph says every post, like and search leaves a trace, and those traces together build up your digital footprint.

g2.correct: what price you see, which news appears first, or which job advert reaches you
accept: what price you see, which news appears first, or which job advert reaches you
g2.label: 2. Besides showing adverts, what does the text say some companies use your data to decide?
g2.why: The second paragraph names exactly these three examples of decisions companies make from your data, besides which adverts you see.

g3.correct: algorithms trained on biased data quietly reinforcing biased decisions
accept: algorithms trained on biased data quietly reinforcing biased decisions
g3.label: 3. What does “the weaponisation of mathematics” refer to, according to the text?
g3.why: The text defines the phrase directly as algorithms trained on biased data quietly reinforcing biased decisions, often without anyone noticing.

g4.correct: search their own name occasionally and see what strangers can find
accept: search their own name occasionally and see what strangers can find
g4.label: 4. What does the text suggest anyone can do to see what their own digital footprint reveals?
g4.why: The final paragraph recommends searching your own name occasionally to see what strangers can find.

g5.correct: because “easy” describes the action itself, not a judgement of advertisers’ character
accept: because “easy” describes the action itself, not a judgement of advertisers’ character
g5.label: 5. “It’s easy for advertisers to build a detailed picture…” — why is for used here rather than of?
g5.why: “For” follows adjectives like easy, important or possible that comment on the action, not on the person’s character.

g6.correct: because “careless” judges the companies’ behaviour, not just the action
accept: because “careless” judges the companies’ behaviour, not just the action
g6.label: 6. “It was careless of many early tech companies not to test their algorithms…” — why is of used here rather than for?
g6.why: “Of” follows adjectives like careless, foolish or kind that judge the person’s (or company’s) behaviour, not just describe the action.

g1.label: 1. It’s easy ___ hackers to find weak passwords that people reuse.
g1.why: “Easy” comments on how simple the action is, not on the hackers’ character, so it takes “for”.

g2.label: 2. It was careless ___ her to post her exact location while on holiday.
g2.why: “Careless” judges her behaviour, so it takes “of”, not “for”.

g3.label: 3. It’s important ___ companies to explain how they use customer data.
g3.why: “Important” describes the action itself, not anyone’s character, so it takes “for”.

g4.label: 4. It was foolish ___ him to click a link from an unknown sender.
g4.why: “Foolish” judges his behaviour, so it takes “of”, not “for”.

g5.label: 5. It’s essential ___ young people to think about their online reputation.
g5.why: “Essential” describes the action itself, not anyone’s character, so it takes “for”.

g6.label: 6. It was sensible ___ the school to teach students about phishing.
g6.why: “Sensible” judges the school’s behaviour, so it takes “of”, not “for”.

g7.label: 7. It’s possible ___ a stranger to find your address from careless posts.
g7.why: “Possible” describes the action itself, not anyone’s character, so it takes “for”.

g8.label: 8. It was greedy ___ the app to ask for so many permissions.
g8.why: “Greedy” judges the app’s (its maker’s) behaviour, so it takes “of”, not “for”.

g1.label: 1. The app made him ___ the cookie settings before he could continue.
g1.why: “Make” is followed by the bare infinitive (no “to”) when it means force someone to do something.

g2.label: 2. She had her old accounts ___ after the data breach.
g2.why: “Have” takes the past participle when the action is done to something of yours by someone else — here, her accounts were deleted by someone else.

g3.label: 3. Our IT teacher made us ___ a video about phishing scams.
g3.why: “Make” is followed by the bare infinitive (no “to”) when it means force someone to do something.

g4.label: 4. He had his password ___ as soon as he noticed something suspicious.
g4.why: “Have” takes the past participle when the action is done to something of yours by someone else — here, his password was changed by someone else (or a service).

g5.label: 5. My parents won’t let me ___ photos that show our exact location.
g5.why: “Let” is followed by the bare infinitive (no “to”) when it means allow someone to do something.

g6.label: 6. The company makes its staff ___ a cybersecurity course every year.
g6.why: “Make” is followed by the bare infinitive (no “to”) when it means force someone to do something.

g7.label: 7. She finally had her phone’s privacy settings ___ by someone who understood them.
g7.why: “Have” takes the past participle when the action is done to something of yours by someone else — here, the settings were checked by someone else.

g8.label: 8. Review — My friend told me that she ___ public Wi-Fi for online banking.
g8.why: This reviews reported speech from 10g-growing-up-black: a present-tense statement (“I never use…”) shifts back to the simple past (“she never used…”) when reported.
